Wren telephoned the Portland number on Corwin Pell's card at seven in the morning, because she wanted to do it before she lost her nerve and because she suspected he was a man who was already at his desk.

He was. "Miss Halloway. That was quick."

"The answer is no."

A pause, long enough that she could hear a radio somewhere in his office playing classical music. "You understand that I'm not going away."

"I understand you have until the thirtieth of June to collect your money," she said. "You'll have it."

"With respect, you don't have it."

"Then you'll have most of it, and we'll talk about the rest. But you won't have the pier." She hung up before he could answer, and then she stood in the office with her heart going like a two-stroke engine, astonished at herself.

Jonah Marsh was waiting on the pier when she came out. He had heard her through the window; everyone always heard everything through that window.

"You turned him down," he said.

"I did."

"Your father would've done the same." He said it simply, the way he said everything. "How're you going to pay?"

She told him: every crossing, the sunset cruises, the charters, the skiff and the spare outboard. Seven days a week through June. He listened, nodding, rolling an unlit cigarette between his fingers.

"Can't run seven days with one deckhand," he said. "Coast Guard won't stand for it, and neither will my back."

"I know. I'll find someone."

"Until you do, I'll pull doubles." He put the cigarette behind his ear. "No extra pay. Not till you're square."

"Jonah, I can't ask—"

"You didn't." He glanced toward the end of the pier, where the tide was slack and the gulls were quarreling over something dead. When he spoke again his voice was lower. "Tomorrow's still on. Six o'clock, after the last run, at the office. I've got something to show you, too, not just tell. Something your father gave me to hold." He looked at her hard. "Don't tell anybody I'm coming. Not Ada. Nobody."

"I won't."

"Tomorrow, then." He went down to the boat to check the bilge, and she watched him go, and the brass key in her cardigan pocket felt suddenly heavier.

They ran four crossings that day. Wren sold eighteen tickets for the first Saturday sunset cruise to a bus tour from Bangor by lunchtime, and she put a hand-lettered sign in the office window, *DECKHAND WANTED — INQUIRE WITHIN*, and by evening she was so tired that her eyes kept sliding off the manifest.

She was locking the office at dusk when she saw the figure at the head of the pier.

He stood under the single sodium lamp with a duffel bag at his feet, a tall man in a Navy surplus jacket, hands jammed in his pockets, looking down the length of Halloway Pier as if measuring it against something he remembered. He had gotten thin. He had a beard now, going gray at the chin, which was impossible, because he was only thirty-one.

"You left a message," Tobias said.

Wren held the office keys so hard they bit her palm. "You didn't call back."

"I'm terrible on the phone." He picked up the duffel. "Is that sign in the window serious? Because I can tie a bowline and I work cheap."

She had rehearsed, over ten years, a great many things to say to her brother if she ever saw him again. None of them came out. What came out was: "You missed the funeral."

"I know." He didn't look away. "I'm here now. That's what I've got."

She looked at him for a long time under the buzzing lamp. Then she unlocked the office door again, because it was cold, and because whatever else he was, he was the only other person alive who had been raised on this pier.
